2	\section{Conclusion}
3	
4	We presented a factorial study of auxiliary spatial supervision during VLA fine-tuning, bridging the gap between spatial VLA methods and behavioral safety evaluation. The best configuration---detached gradients with LayerNorm---reliably outperforms the Vanilla baseline (CAR $0.802$ vs.\ $0.745$; Hedges' $g{=}1.89$, bootstrap 95\% CI for $\Delta$: $[0.025, 0.089]$). A $2{\times}2$ factorial reveals two additive mechanisms: gradient flow under BatchNorm is associated with reduced collision avoidance ($g{=}{-}0.78$); LayerNorm provides a 3.5--4.8\,pp safety advantage ($g{\approx}0.88$). The two protections are complementary ($\eta^2_\text{interaction}{<}0.01$). Spatial label content showed no detectable effect (observed under v1 codebase).
5	
6	Three guidelines follow: (1)~block auxiliary gradients under BatchNorm; (2)~use LayerNorm if gradient flow is desired; (3)~no ground-truth labels are needed---the head is discarded at inference. The additive decomposition ($p_{\text{interaction}}{=}0.76$) could not have been reached by single-factor ablations. Safety depends on optimization dynamics, not spatial content; future work should verify the BN hypothesis directly and extend to other VLA architectures.
7

1	
2	\section{Limitations}
3	
4	All experiments use a single architecture (OpenVLA-OFT, LoRA rank~32) on one benchmark (SafeLIBERO Level~I) in simulation; generalization to other VLAs, full fine-tuning, and real-world settings remains open. The factorial uses $n{=}3$--$4$ seeds per cell; ANOVA results are exploratory. The auxiliary loss weight ($\lambda_0{=}0.01$) was not swept, and the BN running-statistics hypothesis (\S\ref{sec:discussion}) was not directly verified. Codebase sensitivity (\S\ref{sec:mechanism}) implies that quantitative results may not transfer without controlled replication.
5

tool_args.new_string:
\section{Conclusion}

We presented the first factorial study of auxiliary spatial supervision during VLA fine-tuning, bridging the gap between the growing spatial VLA literature and behavioral safety evaluation. The best configuration---detached gradients with LayerNorm---reliably outperforms the no-auxiliary baseline with a large effect size, while the naive default of BatchNorm with gradient flow actually reduces safety below baseline. A factorial analysis reveals that these two protections combine independently, each contributing a meaningful safety improvement.

These findings carry a broader message for the spatial VLA community. The fifteen-plus methods that augment VLAs with occupancy, depth, or point-cloud prediction all assume that richer spatial representations yield better behavior. Our results suggest this assumption is incomplete: the content of spatial labels has no detectable effect on collision avoidance, while optimization-level choices---normalization type and gradient routing---dominate the safety outcome. This redirects attention from \emph{what} the auxiliary head predicts to \emph{how} it interacts with the shared encoder during training.

Three practical guidelines emerge, all at zero inference cost since the auxiliary head is discarded after training. First, do not route auxiliary gradients through a BatchNorm-based encoder---detach them. Second, if gradient flow is desired for other reasons, switch to LayerNorm, which eliminates the safety penalty. Third, ground-truth spatial labels are unnecessary; even random labels achieve comparable outcomes, removing any additional annotation burden.

Future work should directly verify the BatchNorm running-statistics hypothesis through controlled experiments, such as freezing running statistics or comparing train-mode versus eval-mode normalization. Extending the study to other VLA architectures and full fine-tuning regimes would test the generality of these findings. Finally, integrating the auxiliary-head approach with complementary runtime safety methods could yield a more complete safety framework for deployed VLA systems.

We presented the first factorial study of auxiliary spatial supervision during VLA fine-tuning. Detached gradients with LayerNorm reliably outperforms the no-auxiliary baseline, while BatchNorm with gradient flow reduces safety below it. The two protections combine independently, and the content of spatial labels has no detectable effect---redirecting attention from \emph{what} the auxiliary head predicts to \emph{how} it interacts with the shared encoder during training.

The two protections combine independently, and the content of spatial labels has no detectable effect---redirecting attention from \emph{what} the auxiliary head predicts to \emph{how} it interacts with the shared encoder during training.

Three guidelines follow, all at zero inference cost: detach auxiliary gradients under BatchNorm; use LayerNorm if gradient flow is needed; ground-truth spatial labels are unnecessary. Future work should verify the BatchNorm running-statistics hypothesis, extend to other VLA architectures and full fine-tuning, and integrate with runtime safety methods.

tool_args.new_string: \textbf{Safety--success dissociation.} Full OCC (BN) achieves $\text{TSR}{=}0.854$ while exhibiting the worst CAR ($0.725$): safety and task success respond differently to auxiliary supervision~\cite{li2026spatialforcing, yuan2025depthvla, wu2025spatialvla, liu2025occvla}. This dissociation is practically consequential: standard task-success benchmarks, widely used to evaluate spatial VLA methods, cannot serve as proxies for safety. A method that improves manipulation metrics may simultaneously degrade collision avoidance, underscoring the need for independent safety evaluation when deploying VLAs with auxiliary heads.
